questions.q: According to this lesson's validation gate, which IOCs from Lesson 15's scoring pass are eligible to reach a live detection rule or watchlist?
options: Only IOCs tagged auto_promote — analyst_review and archive-tier IOCs stop before this point
Every IOC pulled from any feed, regardless of score
Only IOCs that came from a CSV feed, never from STIX/TAXII
Only IOCs with an even-numbered confidence score
questions.explain: promotable() filters for the auto_promote tag specifically; everything scored lower (analyst_review, archive) is excluded from reaching production detection.

questions.q: Why does the lesson write the auto_promote filter as its own named function, promotable(), instead of inlining the condition wherever it's needed?
options: Named functions run faster than inline conditionals in Python
It allows the function to be converted automatically into a KQL query
It is required syntax for the Sentinel watchlist API
So the intent is obvious in a code review, making it much harder for someone to accidentally wire an unscored, raw feed pull straight into production later
questions.explain: Making the gate its own named function keeps the validation logic visible and reviewable, rather than letting a shortcut quietly skip scoring in some other code path.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the `expires_at` field written alongside each promoted IOC in push_to_detection_watchlist()?
options: It sets how often the KQL analytics rule itself is allowed to run
It is a required field for authenticating to the Sentinel REST API
It records which Python developer pushed the IOC
It gives a pruning job a timestamp to check so stale IOCs can be removed later, preventing the watchlist from growing into an unmaintained graveyard of long-dead infrastructure
questions.explain: Without an expiration path, a promoted-IOC watchlist only ever grows; expires_at is what prune_expired() uses to age entries back out automatically.

questions.q: In the example analytics rule's KQL, what does referencing `_GetWatchlist('detection-promoted-iocs')` by name (rather than embedding a static IOC list in the query) actually buy you?
options: It makes the query run entirely offline, with no connection to Log Analytics
The Python pipeline can update what the rule fires on just by updating the watchlist — the analytics rule itself never needs to be touched or redeployed to pick up newly promoted intel
It automatically encrypts the watchlist contents at rest
It removes the need for the dedupe step from Lesson 13
questions.explain: Because the rule queries the watchlist by name, updating the watchlist through the pipeline is sufficient to change detection behavior — no rule edit or redeploy required.

questions.q: In the end-to-end pipeline shown at the end of this lesson (pull → normalize → dedupe → tag → score → promote → prune), which lesson in this chapter introduced the dedupe step?
options: Lesson 16 (this lesson)
Lesson 15, Scoring and Prioritizing Threat Intel
Lesson 13, Pulling and Normalizing IOC Feeds in Python
Lesson 14, Automating IOC Lookups Against a SIEM
questions.explain: dedupe() was introduced in Lesson 13 alongside the normalize_*() functions, collapsing repeated IOCs across multiple feeds before any lookup, scoring, or promotion happens.
